summary: Customer wants an initial spectroscopy concept and a practical comparison experiment for earlier information about composition changes in an opaque, concentrated milk product on a processing line, while retaining laboratory checks.

facts_stated.text: Customer produces an opaque, concentrated milk product.
The product flows through a processing line.
They currently sample it for fat and protein analysis.
facts_stated.enquiry_quote: We currently sample it for fat and protein analysis

facts_stated.text: They want earlier information about composition changes.
Product temperature and texture vary during production.
facts_stated.enquiry_quote: Product temperature and texture vary during production

facts_stated.text: They want to retain laboratory checks.

customer_premises.claim: Spectroscopy can provide earlier information about composition changes than the current sampling and laboratory checks.
An initial spectroscopy concept can be defined before the deciding facts are known.
A practical comparison experiment can be designed without specifying target ranges, accuracy, detection limits, or response time.
Laboratory checks will remain suitable as a reference while the spectroscopy concept is tested.

unknowns: Target species and concentration ranges for fat and protein.
Required accuracy, precision, detection limit, and response time.
What specific composition changes must be detected and at what magnitude.
Whether the measurement must be in-line, at-line, or online.
Sample matrix details beyond opaque, concentrated milk product.
Whether the product is always liquid or sometimes paste-like or variable in texture.
Temperature range and how temperature varies during production.
Pressure, flow rate, and installation point on the processing line.
Reference laboratory method details and sampling frequency.
Whether any sample conditioning or dilution is acceptable.
Acceptance criteria for the practical comparison experiment.
